claims.text: The cell is the smallest living unit of the body; every living thing is made of cells.
claims.supporting_quote: Cells, the smallest structures capable of maintaining life and reproducing, compose all living things

claims.text: A tissue is a large group of similar cells that work together.
claims.supporting_quote: organization of a great many similar cells

claims.text: An organ, like the heart or a lung, is made of several different kinds of tissue working together for one job.
claims.supporting_quote: An organ is an organization of several different kinds of tissues

claims.text: An organ system is a team of organs that work together, and it is the most complex level inside the body.
claims.supporting_quote: Systems are the most complex of the component units of the human body.

claims.text: The body has four main kinds of tissue: epithelial (covering and lining), connective, muscle, and nervous.
claims.supporting_quote: There are four main tissue types in the body: epithelial, connective, muscle, and nervous.

claims.text: The skeleton is a hard frame that holds the body up and protects soft organs like the brain, heart and lungs.
claims.supporting_quote: Bones provide a rigid framework, known as the skeleton, that support and protect the soft organs of the body.

claims.text: Most new blood cells are made inside bones, in the soft red marrow.
claims.supporting_quote: Hematopoiesis, the formation of blood cells, mostly takes place in the red marrow of the bones.

claims.text: An adult skeleton usually has 206 named bones.
claims.supporting_quote: The adult human skeleton usually consists of 206 named bones.

claims.text: A joint is a place where two bones meet; joints can be immovable, slightly movable, or freely movable.
claims.supporting_quote: An articulation, or joint, is where two bones come together.

claims.text: Most joints in an adult body, like the knee or elbow, are freely movable.
claims.supporting_quote: Most joints in the adult body are diarthroses, or freely movable joints.

claims.text: Skeletal muscle is attached to bones and moves the body, and you control it on purpose (it is voluntary).
claims.supporting_quote: Thus, these muscles are under conscious, or voluntary, control.

claims.text: Smooth muscle is found in the walls of hollow organs such as blood vessels, the stomach and gut, and the bladder. It works without you thinking about it (it is involuntary).
claims.supporting_quote: found in the walls of the hollow internal organs such as blood vessels, the gastrointestinal tract, bladder, and uterus

claims.text: Cardiac muscle is found in the wall of the heart. It squeezes strongly and in a steady rhythm, and you cannot control it on purpose (it is involuntary).
claims.supporting_quote: The contraction of cardiac muscle is involuntary, strong, and rhythmical.

claims.text: A muscle usually crosses a joint and is tied to bones at each end by tendons. When it tightens, one bone stays mostly still and the other bone moves.
claims.supporting_quote: Typically a muscle spans a joint and is attached to bones by tendons at both ends.

claims.text: The heart has four chambers: two thin-walled atria on top that receive blood, and two thick-walled ventricles below that pump blood out.
claims.supporting_quote: The two ventricles are thick-walled chambers that forcefully pump blood out of the heart.

claims.text: Blood coming back from the body, low in oxygen, enters the right side of the heart, which pumps it to the lungs to pick up oxygen.
claims.supporting_quote: Blood flows from the right atrium to the right ventricle, and then is pumped to the lungs to receive oxygen.
supporting_quotes: The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from systemic veins; the left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins.

claims.text: Blood coming back from the lungs enters the left side of the heart, which pumps it out to the whole body.
claims.supporting_quote: From the lungs, the blood flows to the left atrium, then to the left ventricle.

claims.text: Arteries carry blood away from the heart, and veins carry blood back toward the heart.
claims.supporting_quote: Veins carry blood toward the heart.

claims.text: Capillaries are the smallest and most common blood vessels, and their main job is to swap materials between the blood and the body's cells.
claims.supporting_quote: The primary function of capillaries is the exchange of materials between the blood and tissue cells.

claims.text: Blood carries oxygen from the lungs to the body and carbon dioxide back to the lungs, and it also carries food from digestion, hormones, germ-fighting substances, and wastes.
claims.supporting_quote: transporting oxygen from the lungs to body tissue and carbon dioxide from body tissue to the lungs.

claims.text: For an adult at rest, a heart rate of 60 to 100 beats per minute is normal.
claims.supporting_quote: Most adults have a resting heart rate of between 60 and 100 beats per minute.
claims.note: Re-sourced: the earlier NHLBI heart-beats page gives the 60-100 range without saying 'adults'.

claims.text: Air goes in through the nose or mouth, which warm and wet it, then passes the voice box and travels down the windpipe.
claims.supporting_quote: The air then travels past your voice box and down your windpipe.

claims.text: Inside the lungs the tubes branch into thin bronchioles that end in tiny air sacs called alveoli, where oxygen moves into the blood in the capillaries and carbon dioxide moves out to be breathed away.
claims.supporting_quote: The bronchioles end in clusters of tiny air sacs called alveoli.

claims.text: To breathe in, the diaphragm tightens and the chest gets bigger so air flows into the lungs; to breathe out, the diaphragm relaxes and air is pushed out.
claims.supporting_quote: During inspiration, the diaphragm contracts and the thoracic cavity increases in volume.

claims.text: NCI SEER lists ten major organ systems
claims.supporting_quote: Ten major systems compose the human body
claims.conflict: Sources count organ systems differently; the other position in the ledger is a source this library excludes (see ATTRIBUTION.md), so the text names no count as correct and no item grades a count.

claims.text: Some adults, especially young adults or physically fit people, may normally have slower heart rates.
claims.note: Source says 'people who are young'. In context (the adult range) it means young adults; reworded so it is not read as 'children have slower rates', which is the opposite of true.
claims.supporting_quote: Some people, especially people who are young or physically fit, may normally have slower heart rates.
claims.conflict: Edge of the 60-100 range: kept beside c21 so the tutor never calls a fit learner's slow pulse abnormal. No item grades a single number as abnormal.
